Virginia Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession: What Owners Should Know

Can a squatter take title to a Virginia house?

Only after a very long time. Virginia sets a time limit instead of a simple recipe: no one may enter or sue to recover land unless it is done within fifteen years after the right first accrued to that person or to someone through whom he claims (Va. Code 8.01-236). That limit sits underneath adverse possession. Once an owner's right to recover has run out, a person in long possession can argue the owner is too late.

What kind of possession counts, and what a claimant must prove, comes from court decisions. A Virginia attorney can tell you how those decisions apply to a particular property.

Owners with a legal disability get extra time, but only up to a point. No disability, and no adding together of disabilities, preserves a right to enter or sue for more than twenty-five years after it first accrued, even if the person was disabled the entire time (Va. Code 8.01-237).

Why vacant and inherited houses are at risk

A house nobody checks on is the easiest place for an unwelcome occupant to settle in. Heirs who live out of state, owners in a nursing home, and estates waiting on probate all leave properties empty for months. A vacant house can be anywhere from a dense suburb to a rural mountain parcel, and the risk is the same.

A few low-cost steps help:

  • Post clear no trespassing signs and tell the occupant in writing to leave.
  • Keep dated photos and records of who has keys, utilities, and mail.
  • Pay property tax on time so the house does not also face a delinquency suit.
  • Visit on a schedule, or ask a neighbor or property manager to do so.

Records like these matter later. If a dispute reaches a courtroom, a dated photo showing a locked, empty house is better evidence than a memory.

What an owner can do about an unlawful occupant

The statutes give an owner two court routes. One is a motion for judgment in circuit court when someone makes a forcible or unlawful entry on land, or a tenant keeps possession after the right has expired (Va. Code 8.01-124). The action must be brought within three years after the entry or detainer.

The other is a summons for unlawful detainer. The owner gives a sworn statement of the facts to a magistrate, or to a clerk or judge of a general district court, who issues the summons. It must be served at least 10 days before the return day (Va. Code 8.01-126).

Single-family homes get a faster track. When the owner of a residential single family dwelling files and the court finds all three of the following, an emergency hearing is held as soon as practicable and within 14 days of filing, or at the latest within 30 days:

  • no rental agreement exists or ever existed between the owner and the occupant;
  • the occupant lives there without the owner's permission;
  • the owner gave the occupant written notice to vacate at least 72 hours before filing.

This section has been amended on different effective dates, so ask the court clerk for the current wording before you file.

The court case step by step

An unlawful detainer moves through these stages.

StageWhat happens
NoticeWritten notice to vacate at least 72 hours before filing, for the emergency single family hearing
SummonsIssued on the owner's sworn statement; served at least 10 days before the return day
HearingEmergency hearing within 14 days of filing when the conditions are met, otherwise within 30 days at the latest
JudgmentJudgment for the premises, plus proven damages and rent owed; possession can be ordered at the first hearing
AppealWithin 10 days, with bond posted and writ tax paid within 10 days
EvictionSheriff serves notice at least 72 hours before executing the writ, and not before the 10-day appeal period ends

At the initial hearing the plaintiff can receive a final, appealable judgment for possession and an order of possession. On request, the court may split the case and set a later date, no more than 120 days out, to fix final rent and damages (Va. Code 8.01-128). A winning owner can ask the judge to order the writ of eviction to issue immediately. An indigent defendant does not need to post an appeal bond (Va. Code 8.01-129).

Is staying after being told to leave a crime?

It can be. A person who goes onto or stays on another's land, buildings, or premises after being forbidden to do so, orally, in writing, or by a posted sign, is guilty of a Class 1 misdemeanor (Va. Code 18.2-119). The warning has to come from the owner, lessee, custodian, or their agent.

A criminal charge is a separate matter from the civil case that decides possession. The court process above is what settles who gets the property. Owners should not change locks or remove belongings on their own, because the lawful path is the sheriff acting on a writ.

Former owners after a foreclosure

A former owner who is still in a single-family home on the day of a foreclosure sale becomes a tenant at sufferance. The new owner can end that tenancy with a written termination notice given at least three days before the termination date, then file an unlawful detainer. Fair market rent is owed from the foreclosure date until the person leaves, plus damages, reasonable attorney fees, and court costs (Va. Code 8.01-126).

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Virginia houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling a house with an occupant problem

It affects price, timing, and who will buy. A buyer who needs a loan generally needs the home empty and open to inspection, and an open court case can delay that. A cash buyer who purchases as-is can sometimes take the property with the occupant issue still pending, so ask any buyer whether they will do that and who handles the legal filing.

The seller stays responsible for taxes until closing. If the house is behind on tax, the lien ranks ahead of other liens, and a long delinquency can lead to a judicial sale, so a tax payoff may be part of the same closing.

Before choosing a path, write down every fact about how the person got in: any lease, any text or email giving permission, the dates, and what you have done to demand that they leave. A short consultation with a Virginia attorney can tell you whether to file for unlawful detainer first or negotiate a move-out date.

Frequently asked questions

How many years does adverse possession take in Virginia?

The underlying time limit is fifteen years from when an owner's right to enter or sue first accrued. Court decisions decide what a claimant must prove, so talk to a Virginia attorney about specific facts.

Can I change the locks and remove a squatter myself?

Do not count on it. Owners have court routes, a motion for judgment in circuit court or a summons for unlawful detainer, and the sheriff carries out an eviction under a writ. Ask an attorney before taking any step yourself.

How fast can an unlawful detainer be heard?

For a single-family home with no rental agreement, no permission, and a 72 hour written notice, an emergency hearing is set within 14 days of filing, or within 30 days at the latest.

What if the occupant appeals?

An appeal to circuit court must be taken within 10 days, with bond and the writ tax paid in that time, and the sheriff cannot evict before the 10 days end. Indigent defendants need not post a bond.

Can I sell a house with an unwelcome occupant?

Yes, but expect the occupant to affect buyers and timing. As-is buyers may accept that risk, and your closing agent will need a clear plan for possession.

content:
Virginia Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights: Rules for Selling a Rental

Selling a Virginia House? Get a Cash Offer

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Virginia?
We buy Virginia houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

Paperwork a landlord owes a new tenant

Every new tenant is entitled to a written rental agreement and to the statement of tenant rights and responsibilities from the Department of Housing and Community Development. The duty comes from Va. Code 55.1-1204.

Both sides sign an acknowledgment form showing the tenant got the statement. A tenant who refuses to sign leaves the landlord to record the date or dates the form was provided and that the tenant did not sign. Within 10 business days of the effective date, the tenant receives a copy of the signed agreement and the statement.

Skipping the delivery does not void the lease. It does bar the landlord from filing or continuing any action for an alleged lease violation, an unlawful detainer included, until the tenant has the statement. An owner preparing to sell a rented house should check the file for that signed acknowledgment first.

When there is no written lease

If the landlord never offers a written agreement, the same section creates a tenancy by operation of law with fixed terms. Anyone who finds an oral arrangement on a rental, whether buying or selling, should know these defaults.

  • The chapter applies to the unit, and the term is 12 months with no automatic renewal, except in month-to-month cases.
  • Rent is paid in 12 equal installments at the agreed amount, or at fair market rent if none was agreed.
  • Rent is due on the first of the month and is late after the fifth.
  • A deposit of up to two months of rent may be collected.
  • A written agreement can be signed at any point during the 12 months.

When rent is paid weekly, the tenancy is week-to-week. Every other case is month-to-month unless the agreement says otherwise.

Late fees and payment methods

A landlord may charge a late fee only when the written agreement provides for one, and the fee cannot be more than the lesser of 10 percent of the periodic rent or 10 percent of the balance due.

Rent and deposits must be accepted by check and money order, and cash or money order payments earn a written receipt. Collection or processing fees are barred unless a no-fee alternative is offered. Any fee that is charged for card or electronic payment is capped at the actual out-of-pocket cost billed by a third party. A landlord with four or fewer rental units does not have to accept debit or credit cards.

Tenants can ask in writing for a statement of charges and payments. The landlord has 10 business days to provide it, covering the tenancy or the past 12 months, whichever is shorter. A seller can use that same statement to show a buyer exactly what each tenant has paid, which settles most questions about back rent before closing.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Virginia house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Landlords with more than four rentals

An owner of more than four rental units, or of more than a 10 percent interest in more than four, faces added notice rules for renewals. They are in subsection K of 55.1-1204 and summarized here.

RuleVersion now in forceVersion effective July 1, 2027
Rent increase noticeWritten notice at least 60 days before the term endsWritten notice at least 90 days before the term ends, with a reply deadline at least 30 days after delivery
Nonrenewal noticeAt least 60 days before the term endsAt least 60 days before the term ends
Payment plan for small rent balancesNot requiredRequired before the 14-day rent notice in certain cases (55.1-1245)

Neither notice rule covers a periodic tenancy created by operation of law under subsection C of 55.1-1253. A person renting out one house is probably outside these provisions. Someone selling several houses from a portfolio should treat them as live.

Security deposits

A landlord may not demand or take a deposit larger than two months of periodic rent. Deductions must be itemized in writing within 45 days after the tenancy ends or the tenant leaves, whichever comes last. The rules are in Va. Code 55.1-1226.

  • Allowed deductions: accrued rent and late charges, damage beyond reasonable wear and tear, other charges in the lease, and actual damages for breach.
  • With more than one tenant, the refund is a single check payable to all of them, unless they agreed otherwise in writing.
  • With no forwarding address, the landlord may hold the money and, one year past the 45 days, send it to the State Treasurer as unclaimed property.
  • A reasonable part may be withheld for unpaid water, sewer, or other utility bills if prior written notice was given. A tenant who proves payment gets that money back.
  • Records of deductions are kept for two years and open to the tenant during business hours.
  • Damage insurance may be offered in place of a deposit if it meets the listed criteria.

A tenant can ask to be present at the move-out inspection, which must take place within 72 hours of delivering possession. When a landlord willfully fails to comply, the court orders the deposit returned with actual damages and reasonable attorney fees. If the tenant owes rent, the deposit is credited against it.

Deposits when the rental is sold

Whoever holds the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends is bound by the deposit statute and must return any deposit duly owed. That holds however the interest was acquired, whether or not the deposit was handed over, and whatever the old and new owners agreed between themselves.

A seller can prepare in a few steps:

  • List every deposit held and who paid it.
  • Gather the itemized deduction records for the last two years.
  • Get the buyer's written agreement on how deposits are credited at closing, and confirm the tenant is told.
  • Keep the signed rights acknowledgment and the lease together for the buyer.

These are ideas for organizing the file, not legal advice. An attorney should review the closing paperwork.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Virginia houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Landlord remedies after the lease ends

After termination, 55.1-1251 gives the landlord a claim for possession and rent, and a separate claim for actual damages, attorney fees, and service costs. Damages may reach rent through the end of the term or the start of a new tenancy. The landlord must mitigate, and a post-possession judgment cannot seek accelerated rent.

When the tenant moves out by choice or by writ, the deposit is credited under the 45-day rule described above.

A tenant facing a termination notice can often resolve the problem by paying or correcting the breach in time, so reading the notice closely matters. A cash buyer can close on a rented house as-is, and the paperwork above is what a buyer will want to see.

Frequently asked questions

What is the most a landlord can take as a security deposit?

Two months of periodic rent. Deductions must be itemized and the balance returned within 45 days after the tenancy ends or the tenant leaves, whichever is last.

Can a landlord charge any late fee?

Only if the written lease provides for one, and it cannot exceed the lesser of 10 percent of the periodic rent or 10 percent of the balance owed.

Does a missing tenant rights form void the lease?

No. The lease stays valid, but the landlord cannot file or maintain an unlawful detainer for an alleged lease violation until the tenant has the statement of rights and responsibilities.

What are the default terms with no written lease?

A 12-month tenancy with no automatic renewal, rent due on the first and late after the fifth, and a deposit of up to two months of rent. Weekly payers are week-to-week.

Who returns the deposit after a sale?

The holder of the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends. That holder is bound even if the deposit never transferred with the property.

title: Virginia Eviction Notice Rules: Notice Types, Days and Selling the House
content:
Virginia Eviction Notice Rules: Notice Types, Days and Selling the House

Cash Home Buyers in Virginia
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Virginia Eviction Notice Rules: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Virginia Eviction Notice Rules sale
  • Turn the Virginia Eviction Notice Rules offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Virginia House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Virginia?
We buy Virginia houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Notice periods by situation

The right notice depends on the reason for ending the tenancy. Without a proper termination notice admitted into evidence, no judge will enter an order of possession. Missed rent, a breached lease term, and a month-to-month ending all use separate timelines.

SituationNotice periodCode section
Unpaid rent14 days after written notice to pay55.1-1245(F)
Breach that can be fixedLease ends no sooner than 30 days after receipt if not fixed in 21 days55.1-1245(A)
Breach that cannot be fixedNo sooner than 30 days after receipt55.1-1245(C)
Criminal or willful act threatening health or safetyImmediate termination and a possession case55.1-1245(C)
Week-to-week tenancy7 days before the next rent due date55.1-1253(A)
Month-to-month tenancy30 days before the next rent due date, unless the lease says otherwise55.1-1253(A)

The nonpayment notice

Written notice goes to the tenant saying rent is overdue and the lease will end unless it is paid in 14 days. The landlord can terminate only if the money is still missing at the end of that period.

The same 14-day route covers a bounced rent check or an electronic payment rejected for insufficient funds. The notice then has to require payment in cash, by cashier's or certified check, or through a completed electronic transfer.

A rule change takes effect July 1, 2027. After that date a landlord who owns more than four rental units in Virginia, or holds more than a 10 percent interest in more than four, must first send a notice with the exact amount owed when the debt is no more than one month's rent plus contracted late charges. That notice has to offer a payment plan lasting the lesser of six months or the time left on the lease, and the landlord only has to make the offer once during the lease term.

  • Until July 1, 2027: a 14-day written notice, then a possession case under 55.1-1251.
  • From July 1, 2027: larger landlords add the exact-amount notice and the payment plan offer.
  • Late fees stop accruing on the covered debt while the tenant keeps up with the plan.

When a tenant breaks other lease terms

If the tenant can correct the problem, the landlord serves a notice naming the acts or omissions. It says the lease will end on a date at least 30 days after receipt unless the breach is remedied within 21 days. A tenant who fixes it before that date keeps the lease.

A repeat of a similar breach after the first was fixed lets the landlord serve a notice that refers back to the earlier breach. That notice ends the lease no sooner than 30 days after receipt, and no new cure period applies.

Serious conduct gets harsher treatment. Illegal drug activity involving a controlled substance, or another criminal or willful act that threatens health or safety, is an immediate nonremediable violation. That holds even when the tenant did not personally act, because a tenant is presumed to know about activity by an authorized occupant, guest, or invitee unless the tenant proves otherwise. The landlord need not wait for a criminal conviction. The court sets an initial hearing within 15 calendar days of service, and a later hearing or trial follows within 30 calendar days of service.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Virginia house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

The court process after notice

Once the notice period passes, the landlord files a sworn statement and obtains a summons for unlawful detainer from a magistrate, clerk, or judge of the general district court. In residential cases the first hearing should land within 21 days of filing, or 30 days at the latest if the court cannot hear it sooner.

The tenant must be served at least 10 days before the return day. The landlord can ask for all rent due as of the hearing date and may amend the figure if more comes due before the case ends. Rent is not prorated to the hearing date when the lease makes rent due on the first for the whole month and the landlord asks for the full month.

Steps in order:

  • File the sworn statement and get the summons.
  • Serve the tenant at least 10 days before the return date.
  • Attend the first hearing, held within 21 days of filing or 30 at the latest.
  • Present the termination notice and the lease. Photocopies are allowed with an affidavit.

If the judge grants possession, the writ of eviction can be ordered to issue right away when the landlord asks. The summons also warns that an employer may not punish a tenant for missing work to come to court.

Appeal time and the sheriff's writ

Ten days is the window to appeal a general district court judgment to the circuit court, and no eviction can happen before it closes. To appeal, the tenant posts a bond and pays the writ tax inside those same 10 days. Indigent defendants are excused from the bond.

With a writ in hand, the sheriff owes the tenant at least 72 hours of notice of the date and time. Issuance must come within 180 days of the possession judgment, and the writ goes back within 30 days. If 30 days pass without execution, the writ is vacated automatically.

A fresh written lease signed after the judgment means no writ issues.

Occupants with no lease and former owners after foreclosure

Two other situations have their own rules. First, a person living in a single-family home with no rental agreement and no permission. If the owner proves both and gave written notice to vacate at least 72 hours before filing, the court sets an emergency hearing within 14 days, or 30 days at most.

Second, a former owner who stays in a single-family home through the foreclosure sale. That person becomes a tenant at sufferance. The new owner gives written notice at least three days before the effective date and then files for unlawful detainer. Fair market rent runs from the sale date, with damages, attorney fees, and court costs on top.

Squatting and adverse possession are a separate legal question, covered on another page of this site.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Virginia houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What the landlord can recover

On top of possession, the landlord may ask for back rent, actual damages, reasonable attorney fees, and service costs. Code 55.1-1251 does not let the landlord collect accelerated rent for the rest of the term after possession, and damages must be mitigated.

One judgment can cover both money and possession without crediting the security deposit. Once the tenant leaves, the deposit is applied under the Virginia deposit rules.

Holding over after the lease ends without consent exposes the tenant to a suit for possession and actual damages. A lease can fix liquidated damages at up to 150 percent of daily rent per day of holdover; public and HUD-regulated housing is capped at plain daily rent.

Selling a rental during an eviction

Owners who want out of a rental cannot skip the process above: the tenancy is either honored or ended through the courts. Serving a notice leaves the tenant in place, and only the sheriff can execute a writ. Buyers ask where the tenant stands, so organized records save time.

Gather this first:

  • Dates of every notice sent, plus a case number if a case exists.
  • What the tenant has paid and the amount behind.
  • The lease, rent receipts, damage records, and photos.

As-is purchases are our business, whether the rental is occupied or vacant and needs work. Tell us the situation and we will say what we can offer. Whether a given notice is valid is a question for a Virginia landlord-tenant attorney or legal aid.

Frequently asked questions

What notice comes before an unpaid-rent eviction?

Written notice with a 14-day wait for payment comes before termination and a possession case, under Code 55.1-1245(F).

Ending a month-to-month tenancy takes what notice?

Written notice from either side, at least 30 days ahead of the next rent due date, unless the agreement sets something else (Code 55.1-1253).

Can a landlord evict right away for criminal activity?

In limited cases, yes. A criminal or willful act threatening health or safety, including illegal drug activity, allows immediate termination and a possession case. No conviction is needed first.

What is the appeal deadline for a tenant?

Ten days to appeal to the circuit court. The sheriff cannot evict while that period runs (Code 8.01-129).

How long does a writ last?

It must issue within 180 days of the possession judgment and be executed within 30 days of issuance, or it is vacated (Code 8.01-471).
